analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to get customers' opt-out consent before sharing personal financial data with affiliates.
analysis.headline: The Financial Information Privacy Protection Act of 2001 was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, never received a markup or floor vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, the 1999 law that governs how banks handle customer data. Under current law, banks must let customers opt out of having their personal information shared with outside companies, but not with the bank's own corporate affiliates — so a bank holding company can freely share your account records, spending patterns, and other data across its family of companies. This bill would have extended that opt-out right to affiliate sharing, banned banks from selling or transferring lists of individual customers' transactions and preferences, barred banks from using health information to decide whether to offer you credit, prohibited disclosure of account numbers, given consumers the right to see and correct their records, and let state attorneys general enforce the rules in court. It never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary financial consumers: anyone with a bank account, credit card, or brokerage account would gain the right to stop their bank from sharing their personal information with corporate affiliates, the right to see and correct what the bank has on file, and protection from having health information and detailed transaction histories sold or used against them.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the opt-out right under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act to disclosures to corporate affiliates, not just outside third parties, so customers could stop a bank holding company from circulating their records among its own subsidiaries [S2][S3].

Bans banks from transferring individualized lists of a customer's transactions, interests, or preferences — for example, detailed debit and credit card purchase histories — unless the customer affirmatively consents [S2][S3].

Bars banks from obtaining or considering individually identifiable health information when deciding whether, or on what terms, to offer a financial product, unless the customer consents and the bank requires the same information from all applicants [S2][S3].
Prohibits banks from disclosing a customer's account number or access code to an affiliate or third party, a common route to unauthorized account charges [S2][S3].

Gives consumers the right to access and correct the information a financial institution holds about them, and requires privacy notices before a customer relationship begins rather than after [S2][S3].
Adds state attorneys general as enforcers who can sue on behalf of their residents, and makes any violation of a bank's own stated privacy policy an enforceable violation of law [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Financial institutions — banks, credit card issuers, brokerages, and insurance affiliates — would bear compliance costs and lose a lucrative input: the ability to freely pool, analyze, and market against detailed customer data across their affiliates. Data marketers that buy customer lists would lose supply.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose real compliance costs on financial institutions of all sizes, requiring new consent-tracking systems, pre-relationship privacy notices, and customer access-and-correction procedures [S3].

The bill keeps the opt-out model rather than requiring affirmative opt-in consent for most affiliate sharing: customers' data could still flow within a corporate family unless they take action to stop it [S2][S3].

The bill carves out exceptions that allow continued sharing for marketing the institution's own products to its own customers and for consolidated customer service operations like shared call centers and combined statements, limiting how much the opt-out right actually restricts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to consumers are concrete — control over who sees their financial and health information, and enforceable rights to correct it — and the costs are borne mostly by institutions that profit from the current free flow of customer data. The opt-out design and the carve-outs for the bank's own marketing mean the protections are weaker than full consent would provide, but the bill clearly shifts power from institutions to individuals.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Sarbanes introduced the bill on January 22, 2001, joined by six Democratic colleagues, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1][S5].
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup, the Senate never debated it, and there was no floor vote at any point in the two-year Congress [S5].
The bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and was not carried over into the next Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial institutions kept the affiliate data-sharing rights and transaction-marketing flexibility the bill would have restricted, since the opt-out limits of the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act remain the only federal privacy rule for this data. Consumers gained nothing from this attempt.

for.name: Sen. Paul Sarbanes
for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or reported it out during the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Sen. Phil Gramm
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee (at the time of referral)
against.what_they_did: Led the committee that received the bill in early 2001; no action was ever scheduled on it. Gramm was the principal Senate author of the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act the bill would have amended.

against.name: Banking and financial services industry
against.what_they_did: Fought to keep the affiliate-sharing exemption in Gramm-Leach-Bliley and opposed legislation extending opt-out rights to affiliate disclosures.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the Republican-run Banking Committee gave the bill no consideration for the first half of 2001; after Democrats briefly took the committee chairmanship mid-year, the bill still never came up [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Banks and financial institutions (bank holding companies and their affiliates)
industries.note: The bill's core target: it would end the free flow of customer records among a bank holding company's affiliates and ban transfers of transaction histories and account numbers without consent. The industry's current ability to mine and market this data is a revenue source that comes directly at the cost of customer privacy.

The bill bans banks from transferring individualized lists of customers' transactions and preferences — a product these firms buy and resell — and limits redisclosure and reuse of information they do receive. Their business model depends on the data flows the bill restricts.
